docs.title: SurfQuake Plotting and Interactive Commands
docs.text:
SurfQuake provides a powerful plotting interface designed for seismological workflows. It supports trace visualization, interactive pick annotation, metadata overlays, and integration with processing outputs such as characteristic functions, beamforming results, or filtered waveforms.

This plotting interface is designed for both exploratory data analysis and high-quality figure export.

docs.title: Overview of Interactive Plotting
docs.text:
When a waveform stream is visualized (e.g., after running a processing pipeline or with the surfquake quick command), SurfQuake launches an interactive window showing a page of traces. This interface supports keyboard-driven interactions to facilitate manual picking and review.

Each subplot corresponds to a single seismic trace and includes time axes, amplitude plots, and optional overlays (picks, markers, etc.). Traces are paginated if their count exceeds the configured number per page.

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
• Paging: Use n and b to move to next and previous pages.
  • Picking: Press e and click to pick a phase arrival. You'll be prompted for phase type and polarity.
  • Reference markers: Press w to insert a green vertical reference line.
  • Pick management:
  • d: Delete the last pick.
  • c: Clear all picks.
  • m: Remove the most recent reference.
  • p: Remove the last reference marker from all traces.
  • Command prompt: Press v to open the SurfQuake command bar within the plotting session.
  • Exit keys: Use enter or esc to exit the interactive session.

All interactions update the internal Trace.stats metadata. For instance, picks are stored in Trace.stats.picks, and reference markers in Trace.stats.references.

docs.title: Pick Metadata Storage
docs.text:
When a user places a pick using the e key, a dictionary is appended to the picking list tr.stats.picks, with the following structure:

{
    "time": float,          # UTC timestamp
    "phase": str,           # Phase name (e.g., 'P', 'S', 'Pg', etc.)
    "amplitude": float,     # Interpolated amplitude at pick time
    "polarity": str         # 'U', 'D', or '?' (unclear)
}

It is automatically added phase when users pick using shortcut numbers 1-6 (see summary table). Reference markers (green vertical lines placed via w) are stored as timestamps in tr.stats.references.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Make a configuration file (includes full explanation) from the terminal:

surfquake make_config -c plotting_config -o "./"

The plotting interface is governed by a YAML configuration passed via --plot_config, which supports:

plotting:
  traces_per_fig: 3
  sort_by: distance            
  vspace: 0.05
  show_legend: true
  show_help: true
  fast: false
  fast_points: 1000
  back2future: false
  title_fontsize: 9
  plot_type: standard
  record_option: dates
  scale_factor: 1
  sharey: False
  show_arrivals: False
  pick_output_file: ./picks.csv
  auto_load_pick_file: False
  show_info_picks: False
  plot_output_path: False
  show_plot: True
  show_crosshair: false
  plot_output_path: null
  format_save: png
  backend: TkAgg

  • Notes: Specifies how traces are normalized before correlation.

    • traces_per_fig: int. default: 6. Traces per plot

    • sort_by: str|bool default: False. options: 'distance', 'backazimuth', or False. Sort traces y distance, in case you have traces with a editted header or you are running command processing.

    • vspace: float default: 0.05. Vertical space between axis

    • show_legend: bool default: True. If true, show additional information related to the trace.

    • title_fontsize: float default: 9. Size of figure title.

    • plot_type: str. default: 'standard', 'record' for record section and overlay for all traces at the same plot.

    • record_option: str. default: 'dates', 'egf' for specifically display record section the causal and acausal part of Empirical Green Function.

    • scale_factor: float default: 1. Amplitude multiplier of the traces in the record section. Increase it to make the traces overlap neighbours, decrease it to shrink them.

    • sharey: bool. default : False. Share y-axis amplitudes. Useful to compare seismogram amplitudes in many traces

    • pick_output_file: str default "./picks.csv". Path to the file where picks will be written

    • auto_load_pick_file: str|bool default : False. If user wants that picking file is automatically loaded and plot (e.g. picking file NLLoc format)

    • show_info_picks: bool default: False. Show pick info on screen interactively when user pick a phase on the trace.

    • show_crosshair: bool default: False. Show crosshair in all traces. Helps to mark a common reference point and to interactive compare amplitudes.

    • plot_output_path: bool default: False. Path to the output folder in case of Automatic saving plot.

    • show_plot: bool default: True. If set the plot will be display if not and the plot_output_path is True, the plot will be automatically saved with no displaying.

    • backend: str default: TkAgg (maximum robustness, default), MacOSX (only for mac), Qt5Agg (fast, picking & interactive commands raise problems)

    • show_crosshair: bool default: False. Show a crosshair (horizontal + vertical line) following the mouse in every subplot. Useful for precise picking.

    • back2future: bool default: False. Keep a pristine copy of the loaded traces so the interactive command "back2future" can undo all the processing (filter, cut, rotate...). The copy doubles the memory used by the traces and takes some time on large datasets, so it is disabled by default.

docs.title: Output and Persistence
docs.text:
• All user picks and references are stored in memory and (optionally) written to disk.
  • Picks can be logged to CSV using the pick_output_file config key.
  • The waveform figures can be exported as .png files.
  • Header metadata can be updated interactively and saved if exported in HDF5 format.

docs.title: Summary Table of Key Commands in picking mode.
docs.text: Key Action 1 P-wave polarity ? 2 P-wave polarity Up 3 P-wave polarity Down 4 S-wave polarity ? 5 S-wave polarity Up 6 S-wave polarity Down e Add pick (see the terminal) w Add reference line d Delete last pick c Clear all picks m Remove most recent reference p Remove last reference from all n Next page b Previous page v Command prompt enter / esc Exit plotting ---------------------------------------

docs.title: Command-Line Prompt (v Key)
docs.text:
SurfQuake provides an embedded terminal-style command prompt for advanced user interaction. Press v during plotting to access it.

This prompt allows you to apply real-time processing, visualization, trimming, and export actions without leaving the plot.

docs.title: Example Session
docs.text:
>> filter bandpass 0.1 1.0 --corners 4 --zerophase True
>> cut --phase P 5 15
>> beam --method FK --fmin 0.8 --fmax 2.0 --grid 0.05
>> write --folder_path ./processed_h5/
>> p

docs.title: Available Commands (Detailed)
docs.text:
• filter <type> <fmin> <fmax> [options]: Filter all displayed traces.

    • Example: filter bandpass 0.5 8.0 --corners 4 --zerophase True

  • sp <index>|all [axis_type]: Plot spectrum (FFT) of a specific or all traces options of axis plot are loglog, xlog, ylog.

    • Example: spectrum 0, spectrum all loglog

  • spec <index> [win overlap]: Plot multitaper spectrogram of a trace. win is the sliding window defined in seconds and overlap is the % of sliding windoe step overlap.

    • Example: spec 0 4 75 # 4 seconds overalp of 75%

  • cwt <index> <wavelet> <param> [fmin fmax]: Continuous wavelet transform visualization.

    • Example: cwt 1 cm 6 0.1 10 options are wavelet: cm (complex morlet wavelet), mh (mehican hat) and pa (Paul Wavelet).

  • beam [options]: Run beamforming in sliding windows (FK method).

    • Example: beam --fmin 0.5 --fmax 2.5 --win 3 --grid 0.025

  • smap [options]: --fmin --fmax --smax --grid --method FK|MTP.COHERENCE|CAPON|MUSIC

    units: frequency in Hz, smax (maximum slowness search) and grid (Slowness grid spacing) in s/km

    • Example: smap --method CAPON --fmin 1.0 --fmax 3.0 --grid 0.01 smap --method MUSIC --fmin 1.0 --fmax 3.0 --grid 0.01 --nsignals 1

  • stack [options]: list_traces --method [mean|pw|root]

    • Example: stack stack 0,3,7 stack 0-5 --method root:4 stack all --method pw:2

  • xcorr [--ref <i>] [--mode full] [--normalize full]: Apply cross-correlation.

    • Example: xcorr --ref 0 --mode full --normalize full

  • plot_type <type>: Change plot layout (standard, record, overlay).

    • Example: plot_type overlay

  • cut: Trim traces based on:

    • span time selected: cut # cut waveforms according to the starttime and endtime selected by previously draging with right mouse to select start and end time in picking mode.
    • Phase: cut --phase P 5 10 # cut the waveforms 10 seconds before and 20 seconds after the P wave (for traces with picked P wave)
    • Reference marker: cut --reference 10 20 # cut the waveforms 10 seconds before and 20 seconds after the common reference.
    • UTC: cut --start "2024-01-01 12:00:00" --end "2024-01-01 12:01:00" # cut all waveforms acoording to the span time

  • shift --phase <name> or --phase_theo <name>: Time-align traces.

    • shift --phase S # according picked phase S-wave
    • shift --phase_theo S # according to the theoretically estimated S-wave. Only if event info is in header. see surfquake processing -e event

  • concat: Merge overlapping trace segments using interpolation. Merge daily seismograms by net station channel

  • pm: Perform particle motion analysis (Z-N-E style).

  • write --folder_path <path>: Export displayed traces to .h5.

  • info : Print header information from displayed traces

  • p: Return to interactive pick mode.

  • n / b: Navigate to next/previous page.

  • help [command]: Show help or detailed help for a command.

  • exit: End command prompt and close plotting.

Very important: Exit from auxiliary plots, let's say spectrum, spectrogram or cwt by pressing enter / esc, NOT closing the GUI. Otherwise the prompt is frozen an you will not able to back to picking mode.

This system offers a lightweight yet highly customizable interface for interactive seismogram analysis in SurfQuake. It blends visual inspection with real-time metadata editing to support modern waveform workflows.

docs.title: Probability Power Spectral Density Functions (PPSD)
docs.text: The Probability Power Spectral Density Functions (Peterson, 1993; McNamara & Buland, 2004) are used to characterize the background seismic noise.

docs.title: PPSD DB CLI
docs.text:
This command creates a file-based database that stores Probability Power Spectral Density Functions (PPSD) in a pickle file. The file is basically a dictionary with keys net, station channel and the ObsPy object with the PPSD.

        Key Arguments:
            -p,  --project_file        [REQUIRED] Path to project file (previously generated using surfquake project)
            -i,  --inventory_file      [REQUIRED] Path to stations metadata (XML or RESP)
            -s,  --save_file           [REQUIRED] Path to save the data base
            -le, --length              [OPTIONAL] Length of data segments passed to psd in seconds (default 3600)
            -ov, --overlap             [OPTIONAL] Overlap in percentage of segments passed to psd (default 50)
            -sm, --smoothing           [OPTIONAL] PSDs are averaged over a octave at each central freq (default 1)
            -n,  --net                 [OPTIONAL] project net filter (Default: *, Example WM)
            -s,  --station             [OPTIONAL] project station filter (Default: *, Example ARNO)
            -ch, --channel             [OPTIONAL] project channel filter (Default: *, Example BH?)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: >> surfquake ppsdDB -p [project_file] -i [inventory_file] -s [save_file] -le [Time window length] -sm [Smoothing] -ov [Overlap] -pr [Period] -nt [Net Selection]  -st [Station Selection] -ch [Channel Selection]

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake ppsdDB -h

docs.title: Examples CLI
docs.text: >> surfquake ppsdDB -p "./ppsd_test" -i "./meta/metadata.xml" -s "./output/test.pkl"

docs.title: Class
docs.text:
PPSDSurf

class PPSDSurf:
    def __init__(self, files_path: Union[str, SurfProject], metadata: Union[str, Inventory], length=3600, overlap=50, smoothing=1.0, period=0.125):

    """

    PPSDs utils for Surfquake.

    Parameters
    ----------
    files_path : str | SurfProject | dict
        Can be:
        - a filesystem path containing waveform files,
        - a SurfProject instance,
        - a SurfProject.project-like dictionary.
    metadata : str | Inventory
        Dataless / StationXML / ObsPy inventory metadata.
    length, overlap, smoothing, period
        PPSD configuration values.

    """

docs.title: Plotting & Statistics
docs.text: Reads a PPSD pickle database produced by ppsdDB and generates publication-quality figures.

docs.title: PPSD Plot CLI
docs.text:
Three plot modes are available:

    heatmap    Probability density colormaps (classic PPSD view).
               One figure per group of --spp stations.  Use --all to
               iterate automatically over every station group.

    variation  Diurnal or seasonal noise variation shown as a contour
               plot (mode amplitude vs hour-of-day or month).

    comparison Overlay mean / median / mode curves for a wildcard
               selection of stations and channels on shared axes.
               One panel per component (Z, N, E …) or a single panel.

    Key Arguments:
        -d,  --db_file         [REQUIRED] Path to the PPSD pickle database
        -m,  --mode            [REQUIRED] Plot mode: heatmap | variation | comparison
        -sd, --save_dir        [OPTIONAL] Directory to save figures (one per page)
        -sp, --save_path       [OPTIONAL] Single output file path (heatmap p.0 or comparison)
        -sf, --save_format     [OPTIONAL] Figure format: png | pdf | svg          (png)
        -nt, --net             [OPTIONAL] Network wildcard filter                  (*)
        -st, --station         [OPTIONAL] Station wildcard filter                  (*)
        -ch, --channel         [OPTIONAL] Channel wildcard filter, e.g. BH?        (*)
        -t0, --starttime       [OPTIONAL] Start of time window, ISO format
        -t1, --endtime         [OPTIONAL] End of time window, ISO format

      heatmap / variation only:
        --spp                  [OPTIONAL] Stations per page                          (3)
        --page                 [OPTIONAL] Page index (0-based); ignored with --all   (0)
        --all                  [OPTIONAL] Iterate over all station groups
        --variation            [OPTIONAL] Variation type: Diurnal | Seasonal  (Diurnal)
        --mean                 [OPTIONAL] Overlay mean curve
        --mode                 [OPTIONAL] Overlay mode curve
        --nhnm                 [OPTIONAL] Overlay NHNM reference
        --nlnm                 [OPTIONAL] Overlay NLNM reference
        --earthquakes          [OPTIONAL] Overlay earthquake model lines
        --min_mag              [OPTIONAL] Minimum magnitude for eq. models          (0.0)
        --max_mag              [OPTIONAL] Maximum magnitude for eq. models         (10.0)
        --min_dist             [OPTIONAL] Minimum distance for eq. models (km)      (0.0)
        --max_dist             [OPTIONAL] Maximum distance for eq. models (km)   (10000)

      comparison only:
        --stats                [OPTIONAL] Comma-separated list: mean,median,mode   (mean)
        --layout               [OPTIONAL] by_component | single          (by_component)

docs.title: Interactive help
docs.text: >> surfquake ppsdDB -h

docs.title: Examples CLI
docs.text:
>> surfquake ppsdPlot -d "./output/test.pkl" --all -m heatmap --mean --nhnm --nlnm --earthquakes --min_mag 1.0 --max_mag 3.0
>> surfquake ppsdPlot -d "./output/test.pkl" --spp 1 --all -m heatmap --mean --nhnm --nlnm --earthquakes --min_mag 1.0 --max_mag 3.0
>> surfquake ppsdPlot -d "./output/test.pkl" -st "OBS01,OBS02" -m heatmap --mean --nhnm --nlnm --earthquakes --min_mag 1.0 --max_mag 3.0
>> surfquake ppsdPlot -d "./output/test.pkl"  -m variation --variation Diurnal
>> surfquake ppsdPlot -d "./output/test.pkl" -m comparison --mean --nhnm --nlnm

docs.title: Detrending
docs.text:
Remove unwanted trends from the raw signal:

  • linear: Remove a best-fit line
  • demean: Subtract the mean
  • polynomial: Fit and subtract a polynomial (e.g., degree 3)
  • spline: Subtract a smooth spline fit

docs.title: Tapering
docs.text:
Apply a window to reduce spectral leakage near signal edges.

  • Parameter: max_percentage (e.g., 0.05 for 5%)
  • Supported Windows: cosine, hann, hamming, blackman, kaiser, flattop, slepian.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05

docs.title: Normalize
docs.text:
Rescale amplitude:

  • 0: Normalize by maximum
  • Custom value: Divide signal by provided constant
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'normalize'
    norm: True

docs.title: Reverse
docs.text:
Reverse the data points of a seismic trace in-place (time-reversal)

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'reverse'

docs.title: Flip
docs.text:
Simply multiply the trace samples by -1 so that change the polarity

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'flip'

docs.title: Cut
docs.text:
Cut Traces:

  • Parameters: method , start, end,t_before, t_after
  • Optional parameters: pad & fill_value

pad (bool, Default: False). Gives the possibility to trim at time points outside the time frame of the original trace, filling the trace with the given fill_value.

fill_value (int, float or None, Default: None) – Fill value for gaps. Traces will be converted to NumPy masked arrays if no value is given and gaps are present.

  • method:absolute, phase, reference

Cut all traces according to a date using method: absolute and parameters start, end or relative to a phase (i.e 'P'), or the last reference saved in the trace header.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cut'
    method: 'absolute'
    start: 2018-10-26T05:20:03
    end: 2018-10-26T06:25:03

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cut'
    method: 'phase'
    t_before: 10.5
    t_after: 120.0

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Apply filters to isolate specific frequency content.

  • Parameters: freqmin, freqmax, zerophase, corners (poles)
  • Filter Types:
  • bandpass, lowpass, highpass, bandstop
  • Parametric options: cheby1, cheby2, elliptic, bessel

ℹ️ Ensure freqmin < freqmax for band filters.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'normalize'
    norm: True
  process_4:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

docs.title: Wiener Filter
docs.text:
• Parameters: time_window (seconds), noise_power
  • Tip: If noise_power=0, it’s estimated from local variance.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: "wiener_filter"
    time_window: 1.0
    noise_power: 0

docs.title: Wavelet Denoise
docs.text:
• Parameters: wavelet_family (e.g., sym8), threshold (e.g., 0.05)
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.5
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True
  process_4:
    name: 'wavelet_denoise'
    dwt: 'sym8'
    threshold: 0.1

docs.title: Resampling
docs.text:
Adjust the sampling rate (e.g., for standardization):

  • Parameters: new_sampling_rate, pre_filter (recommended: True)
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'resample'
    sampling_rate: 20
    pre_filter: True

docs.title: Quick Resampling
docs.text:
This strategy makes a very fast resampling specially designg to speed up the plot of seismograms. Warning this resampling not prevents from aliasing effects.

  • Parameters: factor, integers (recommended: True)
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'raw'
    factor: 20
    integers: True

docs.title: Fill Gaps
docs.text:
• Methods: interpolate, latest (repeat last value)
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'fill_gaps'
    method: 'latest'

docs.title: Differentiate
docs.text:
Estimate the signal’s derivative:

  • Methods: gradient, spectral
Analysis:
  process_9:
    name: 'differentiate'
    method: 'spectral'

docs.title: Integrate
docs.text:
Reconstruct displacement or velocity:

  • Methods: cumtrapz, spline, spectral
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'integrate'
    method: 'spectral'

docs.title: Time Shifting
docs.text:
Shift traces forward or backward in time.

  • Parameter: List of time shifts in seconds
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'shift'
    time_shifts: [-5, 2] # list of shift seconds of the starttime. 
    phase: P #  if pick is vailable. 
    phase_theo: P #  if your trace header has event information.

docs.title: Remove Instrument Response
docs.text:
Convert raw counts to physical units (e.g., velocity or displacement):

⚠️ WARNING: Remember to includ your inventory: e.g., surfquake quick -w "waveform_file" -i "inventory_file.xml"

  • Parameters: pre_filt (list), water_level, units, inventory
  process_1:
    name: 'remove_response'
    water_level: 90
    units: 'VEL' # [ACC Wood Anderson]
    pre_filt: [0.005,0.008,45,48] # Hz, incremental frequencies defining the pre-filt

docs.title: Add Noise
docs.text:
White Noise: - Parameter: SNR_dB amount of noise relative to maximum amplitude of the original trace.

Colored Noise (optional, not in base config): - Use exponent for control: 0 (white), 1 (pink), 2 (brown), -1 (blue), etc.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'add_noise'
    noise_type: 'white'
    SNR_dB: 1

docs.title: Spectral Whitening
docs.text:
Flattens signal spectrum while preserving phase:

  • Parameters: freq_width (Hz), taper_edge (True/False)
Analysis:
  process_11:
    name: 'whitening'
    fmin: 0.05
    fmax: 24.5
    freq_width: 0.02
    taper_edge: True

docs.title: Time Normalization
docs.text:
Standardize temporal energy distribution:

  • Methods: time-normalization, 1bit, clipping and clipping iteration.
  • Parameters: norm_win, iterations
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'time_normalization'
    method: 'time normalization'
    norm_win: 10

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
Reduce high-frequency noise or jitter:

  • Parameters: time_window, fwhm
  • Methods: mean, gaussian, tkeo
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'smoothing'
    method: 'gaussian'
    time_window: 5
    FWHM: 0.05

docs.title: Spike Removal
docs.text:
Removes isolated outliers using hampel algorithm:

  • Parameters: window_size, sigma (standard deviations from the avarage noise)
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'remove_spikes'
    window_size: 10
    sigma: 4

docs.title: Data Processing with SurfQuake
docs.text:
Welcome to the Signal Processing Module of SurfQuake — a powerful and scalable command-line tool for applying signal processing pipelines to large collections of seismic waveform data.

Whether you're analyzing earthquake catalogs or preparing data for machine learning models, this module allows you to define, control, and automate your signal processing workflow with precision.

📘 Learn more in our Signal Processing Tutorial

Remember that you can use real data files and metadata to learn how to use surfquake processing commands with Case of study.

In the following link, you will find config file templates.

docs.title: Running the Process
docs.text:
This tool runs via the terminal. First in the terminal you can ask for help. Available commands are quick, processing and processing_daily.

surfquake command -h

docs.title: surfquake quick
docs.text:
Let's start explaining quick command:

Overview: Process seismic traces. You can: - Apply processing steps (filtering, normalization, etc.) - Optionally visualize the waveforms (interactive mode) - Apply a user-defined post-processing script before or after plotting

Modes:
    Default  : Interactive mode (plotting + user prompts)
    --auto   : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, outputs written automatically)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use `--post_script` to apply a custom script to each event stream.
    Use `--post_script_stage` to control **when** it runs:
        • before : script runs before plotting (good for filtering, editing headers)
        • after  : script runs after plotting (good if picks or metadata are added)

    Examples:
        Process waveform files with a config and plot interactively:
            surfquake quick -w "./data/*.mseed" -c ./config.yaml -i ./inventory.xml --plot_config plot.yaml

Key Arguments:
        -w, --wave_files         [REQUIRED | OPTIONAL] Glob pattern or path to waveform files, (not needed if the config has a 'Source' section)
        -f, --fast               [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
        -c, --config_file        [OPTIONAL] YAML config defining processing steps
        -i, --inventory_file     [OPTIONAL] Station metadata (StationXML or RESP)
        -o, --output_folder      [OPTIONAL] Directory to save processed traces
        -a, --auto               [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic (non-interactive) mode
        -m, --merge              [OPTIONAL] If merge traces as fist action
        -op, --order_preference  [OPTIONAL] 'trace_first' (default) or 'stream_first' — controls
                                  whether trace-level steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before
                                  or after stream-level steps (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
            --min_date           [OPTIONAL] Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT None
            --max_date           [OPTIONAL] Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT None
            --plot_config        [OPTIONAL] Plotting settings YAML
            --post_script        [OPTIONAL] Python script to apply to each stream
            --post_script_stage  [OPTIONAL] When to run post-script: 'before

docs.title: surfquake processing
docs.text:
Overview:
    Process or cut waveforms associated with seismic events.
    You can:
        - Cut traces using event times and headers
        - Apply processing steps (filtering, normalization, etc.)
        - Optionally visualize the waveforms (interactive mode)
        - Apply a user-defined post-processing script before or after plotting

Modes:
    Default  : Interactive mode (plotting + user prompts)
    --auto   : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, outputs written automatically)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use `--post_script` to apply a custom script to each event stream.
    Use `--post_script_stage` to control **when** it runs:
        • before : script runs before plotting (good for filtering, editing headers)
        • after  : script runs after plotting (good if picks or metadata are added)

Usage Example:
    surfquake processing -p "./project.pkl" -i inventory.xml -e events.xml -c config.yaml -o ./output_folder --phases P,S --plot_config plot_settings.yaml --post_script custom_postproc.py

Key Arguments:
    -p, --project_file         [OPTIONAL] Path to an existing project file
    -w, --wave_files           [OPTIONAL] Path or glob pattern to waveform files
    -f, --fast                 [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
    -i, --inventory_file       [OPTIONAL] Station metadata file (XML, RESP)
    -e, --event_file           [OPTIONAL] Event catalog in txt format (columns: date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude)
    -c, --config_file          [OPTIONAL] Processing configuration file (YAML)
    -a, --auto                 [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic mode
    -o, --output_folder        [OPTIONAL] Folder where processed files are saved
    -n, --net                  [OPTIONAL] Project net filter Example: NET1,NET2,NET3
    -s, --station              [OPTIONAL] Project station filter Example: STA1,STA2,STA3
    -ch, --channel,            [OPTIONAL] Project channel filter Example: HHZ,BHN
    -t, --cut_time             [OPTIONAL] pre & post first arrival in seconds (symmetric)
    -cs, --cut_start_time      [OPTIONAL] Cut pre-first arrival in seconds
    -ce, --cut_end_time        [OPTIONAL] Cut post-first arrival in seconds
    -r, --reference            [OPTIONAL] The pick time for cutting the waveforms is the origin time of the event
    -op, --order_preference    [OPTIONAL] trace_first (default) | stream_first. Controls whether trace-level
                               steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before or after stream-level steps
                               (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
    --phases                   [OPTIONAL] Comma-separated list of phases for arrival estimation (e.g., P,S)
    --vel                      [OPTIONAL] Phase speed to estimate the first arrival time (reference for cutting waveform)
    --plot_config              [OPTIONAL] Optional plot configuration file (YAML)
    --post_script              [OPTIONAL] Python script to apply per event stream
    --post_script_stage        [OPTIONAL] When to apply the post-script: before | after (default: before)

Notes:
You might need to set -w for individual files or -p for loading your project file

docs.title: surfquake processing_daily
docs.text:
This command is different to simply surfquake processing because is intended to merge daily seismograms and work for big data sets. For xample, imagine that you need three days of seismograms for normal modes analysis of an event. Or imagine you would like to process datayo your daily mseed files.

Overview:
    Cut seismograms and apply processing to continuous waveforms.
    You can perform either or both of these operations.

Modes:
    Default : Interactive mode (with plotting and prompts)
    --auto  : Non-interactive mode (no plots, no prompts, automatic output)

Post-Script Logic:
    Use --post_script to apply a custom script per station/day stream.
    Use --post_script_stage to control when the script is applied:
        • before : apply script before plotting (e.g., for filtering or cleanup)
        • after  : apply script after plotting (e.g., to act on manual picks)

Usage Example:
    surfquake processing_daily \\
        -i inventory.xml \\
        -c config.yaml \\
        -o ./output_folder \\
        --min_date "2024-01-01 00:00:00" \\
        --max_date "2024-01-02 00:00:00" \\
        --span_seconds  86400\\
        --plot_config plot_settings.yaml \\
        --post_script my_custom.py \\
        --post_script_stage after

Key Arguments:
    -p, --project_file        [REQUIRED] Path to a saved project files
    -f, --fast                [OPTIONAL] Quick-and-Dirty plotting
    -o, --output_folder       [OPTIONAL] Directory for processed output
    -i, --inventory_file      [OPTIONAL] Station metadata (XML/RESP)
    -c, --config_file         [OPTIONAL] Processing configuration (YAML)
    -a, --auto                [OPTIONAL] Run in automatic mode
    -n, --net                 [OPTIONAL] Network code filter
    -s, --station             [OPTIONAL] Station code filter
    -ch, --channel            [OPTIONAL] Channel filter
    -op, --order_preference   [OPTIONAL] trace_first (default) | stream_first. Controls whether trace-level
                              steps (rmean, filter, taper...) run before or after stream-level steps
                              (cross_correlate, rotate, stack...)
    --min_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter Start date (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT min date of the project
    --max_date                [OPTIONAL] Filter End date   (format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), DEFAULT max date of the project
    --time_tolerance          [OPTIONAL] Tolerance in seconds for time filtering, excluded files with smaller time span
    --span_seconds            [OPTIONAL] Select and merge files in sets of time spans, DEFAULT 86400
    --time_segment            [OPTIONAL] If set, process entire time window as a single merged stream of traces
    --plot_config             [OPTIONAL] Optional plotting configuration (YAML)
    --post_script             [OPTIONAL] Path to Python script for custom post-processing
    --post_script_stage       [OPTIONAL] When to apply the post-script: before | after (default: before)
"""

docs.title: Event File Format (event.txt)
docs.text:
Please find here a very simple event file format. This is typical input for surfquake processing -e ./event.txt

date;hour;latitude;longitude;depth;magnitude
2022-02-02;23:35:29.7;42.5089;1.4293;20.7;1.71
2022-02-03;12:01:21.6;42.3047;2.2741;0.0;1.65

docs.title: Sample Processing Configuration (config.yaml)
docs.text:
The macro configuration (provided via a YAML file) defines your signal processing pipeline in a structured, step-by-step format. Each process entry specifies a method, its parameters, and the order in which it will be applied to each trace. You can process either full daily waveform files or extract and process specific segments based on an event file. Additionally, an interactive plotting tool is available to help you visually inspect and validate the processing steps.

Please find here a very simple event file format. This is the typical input file for this commands:

surfquake quick -w ./mseed_file -c ./config.yaml # reading directly mseed files

surfquake processing -p ./project.pkl -c ./config.yaml -e ./event.txt # loading a project and using event files

config.yaml: Detaled information of this file in Processing traces and Processing Stream.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rmean'
    method: 'linear'
  process_2:
    name: 'taper'
    method: 'cosine'
    max_percentage: 0.05
  process_3:
    name: 'filter'
    type: 'bandpass'
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 8.0
    corners: 4
    zerophase: True

docs.title: Arithmetic Operation
docs.text:
Compute simple arithmetic operations between traces.

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'algebra'
    expression: "tr1 + tr2 - tr3"
    trim: True
    fill_gaps: True
    resample: True

docs.title: Rotate Seismograms
docs.text:
This option rotates the three-component traces in the stream to either the Great Arc Circle (GAC) or a user-defined angle and inclination.

  • type: Defines the rotation transformation.

    • NE->RT: Rotates North and East components to Radial and Transverse.
    • RT->NE: Rotates Radial and Transverse components back to North and East.
    • ZNE->LQT: Rotates from a left-handed Z, North, East system to an LQT (ray-based, right-handed) coordinate system.
    • LQT->ZNE: Rotates from an LQT system back to a left-handed Z, North, East system.

  • method: Specifies the rotation method.

    • GAC: Rotates according to the Great Arc Circle. Requires event metadata.
    • FREE: Rotates to a user-defined angle and inclination (used for LQT transformations).

  • angle (float) – The back azimuth from station to source in degrees.

  • inclination (float). Inclination of the ray at the station in degrees. Only necessary for three component rotations.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'rotate'
    type: 'NE->RT'
    method: 'GAC'
    angle: 30.0
    inclination: 0.0

docs.title: Cross Correlation & Concolution
docs.text:
Performs cross-correlation between waveforms.

  • name: cross_correlate or convolve.

  • mode: Defines how the cross-correlation is computed, following the NumPy correlate method:

    • full: Returns the complete cross-correlation function. Includes all shifts, even partial overlaps. Best if you want to scan the entire signal.
    • valid: Returns only correlation values where the signals fully overlap. Safer when you want to avoid edge effects.
    • same: Returns output of the same length as the input data, centered around zero lag.

  • normalize: Specifies how traces are normalized before correlation. Not applied in convolution

    • full: Uses zero-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). Each point is normalized based on local signal energy and optional demeaning. This provides a correlation coefficient between -1 and 1 and is the most statistically meaningful
    • naive:Normalizes both signals by their global standard deviation. Quicker but may introduce bias if signals have amplitude variation.
    • none: No normalization is applied. Raw amplitudes are used, which may be sensitive to trace scaling or noise.
  • reference_idx: Index of the trace to use as the reference for correlation (typically one of the traces in the stream).
  • strict: If True, enforces strict alignment and compatibility between trace lengths and sampling rates.
  • trim: If True, cut all waveforms for the maxumum start time and minimum end time.
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cross_correlate'
    mode: 'full'
    normalize: 'full'
    reference_idx: 0
    strict: True
    trim: True

docs.title: Stack
docs.text:
Stacks multiple traces using a specified method.

  • method: Specifies the stacking method:

    • linear: Simple arithmetic mean across traces.
    • pw: Phase-weighted stacking, emphasizing coherent phase information. Order 1 is the parameter of this method. Recommended 1.
    • root: nth-root stack

  • order: The exponent applied in phase-weighted stacking. A higher value gives stronger weighting to coherent signals.

  process_1:
    name: 'stack'
    method: 'pw'
    order: 1

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
In many processing workflows, it is necessary to synchronize all traces to a common reference point in time. This ensures consistent alignment for further processing steps such as stacking, correlation, or rotation.

Two synchronization methods are supported:

  • starttime: Aligns all traces to a common absolute start time as defined in their metadata. This method assumes all traces are recorded simultaneously and no additional time correction is needed.

  • MCCC: (Multi-Channel Cross-Correlation): Dynamically aligns traces based on their waveform similarity by computing relative delays. This method maximizes coherence across all channels and is especially effective in noisy conditions or when arrival times differ slightly due to path effects or instrument drift. The MCCC approach is based on: VanDecar, J. C., & Crosson, R. S. (1990).

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'synch'
    method: 'starttime' # or MCCC

docs.title: shift
docs.text:
This method applies temporal alignment to traces in a stream using one of several strategies. It is useful when aligning waveforms for stacking, correlation, or interpretation, and offers flexible options including theoretical models, observed picks, or manual time shifts. Please review traces header info to fully understand this method.

phase_theo: Aligns traces based on theoretical arrival times. The expected arrival must be stored in trace.stats.geodetic['arrivals'] under the specified phase name. Use case: When synthetic or model-based timing is reliable (e.g., teleseismic body waves).

  • phase: Aligns traces to observed picks, typically generated from prior picking routines or manual annotation. Pick information must be stored in trace.stats.picks. Use case: When you trust the quality of observed picks more than theoretical estimates.

  • time_shifts: Applies manual time shifts to each trace, using a list of per-trace time offsets in seconds (float). Use case: When you want full control over the alignment or need to apply empirical or experiment-specific shifts.

  • Optional alternatives:

  • phase: 'P'
  • time_shifts: [0.1, -0.2, 0.05] in seconds

Note: If both phase and time_shifts are provided, phase takes precedence. If none of the options are valid, the stream is returned unchanged. 

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'shift'
    phase_theo: 'P'

docs.title: Concatenate
docs.text:
This method concatenates multiple time-continuous trace segments within the same stream. It is commonly used to join split traces that were originally recorded as separate files or segments (e.g., due to daily files, instrument restarts, or transmission delays). Internally, it uses ObsPy's Stream.merge() functionality with:

method=1: Linear interpolation for filling gaps

fill_value='interpolate': Gaps are filled using interpolated values

Behavior Overlapping traces are merged into a single continuous trace. Gaps are filled using linear interpolation between adjacent segments. Non-overlapping or incompatible traces (e.g. different IDs or sampling rates) are left unmerged.

Note: Trace concatenation is automatically done when command is surfquake process or surfquake process_daily but not for surfquake quick for full control. 

Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'concat'

docs.title: Chop comtinuous data
docs.text:
Chop continuous seismic data into a chunks of specific length.

  • chunk_length: (int|float) Output window length in seconds.
  • min_length: (int|float) Minimum amount of REAL recorded data required, in seconds.
  • max_interpolation_gap: (optional: int|float) Maximum gap that we allow to interpolate, in seconds.
  • output_dir: (str) output path to the traces chopped in mseed files
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'chop'
    chunk_length: 1800.0
    min_length: 1760.0
    output_dir: /continuos/chop_data

docs.title: Create your project
docs.text:
In surfQuake a project is simply a python object that can store the path to valid seismogram files plus the associated metadata in its attributes . This strategy allows to proceed with fast filters or join different projects. Project is the necessary input for the toolboxes Picker, Associator, Event Locator, Seismic Source and MTI.

Here we will explain how the user can manage a project and be ready to proceed with the rest of toolboxes.

docs.text: This command allows you to create a seismic project, which is essentially a dictionary storing the paths to seismogram files along with their corresponding metadata.

docs.title: Custom User Scripts in SurfQuake
docs.text: SurfQuake allows users to inject their own custom Python logic into waveform processing workflows. This functionality is available in both batch processing (surfquake process) and quick interactive workflows (surfquake quick).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
User scripts provide a flexible, programmable interface to manipulate seismic traces beyond standard configuration options. You can implement your own algorythm in the workflow such as:

  • Apply custom filtering, transformations, or corrections
  • Modify or inspect waveform data (tr.data)
  • Inject or update metadata in tr.stats. These scripts have direct access to each trace and its metadata (trace.stats), allowing you to inspect, modify, or annotate data based on custom logic. Be in mind the modified header of traces in surfquake.
  • Run scientific algorithms (e.g., polarization, machine learning)
  • Export trace summaries or diagnostics

docs.title: Script Structure
docs.text: Each script must define a run(stream, **kwargs) function that takes: - stream: an ObsPy Stream object containing the current event or waveform group - kwargs: optional keyword arguments, such as inventory or event info

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def run(stream, **kwargs):
    '''
    User-defined post-processing hook for each event.

    :param stream: obspy Stream
    :param inventory: obspy Inventory (passed via kwargs)
    :param event: dict with keys like origin_time, latitude, longitude, depth (passed via kwargs)
    '''
    inventory = kwargs.pop('inventory', None)
    event = kwargs.pop('event', None)

    if event is not None:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces from event at {event['origin_time']}")
    else:
        print(f"Post-processing {len(stream)} traces (no event info provided)")

    # Example: calculate global mean amplitude
    all_data = np.hstack([tr.data for tr in stream])
    print("Mean amplitude:", np.mean(all_data))

    # Example: apply a simple differencing operator to each trace
    for tr in stream:
        tr.data = np.diff(tr.data)

    return stream

docs.title: surfquake process
docs.text:
surfquake process --config config.yaml --post_script myscript.py
  • Executes your script after all config steps are complete.
  • Useful for event-level operations or header editing before writing to disk.

docs.title: surfquake quick
docs.text:
surfquake quick \
  -w "./data/*.mseed" \
  -i inventory.xml \
  --post_script myscript.py \
  --post_script_stage before
  • --post_script: Path to the user script.
  • --post_script_stage:
  • before: Runs the script before plotting (good for data transforms)
  • after: Runs after plotting (useful if user interaction modifies data)

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always return the modified stream from run().
  • Use tr.stats to store temporary or derived metadata.
  • Print useful info for logging/debugging.
  • Test your script independently before integrating it into batch workflows.

docs.title: Advanced Use
docs.text:
You may combine user scripts with processing configs to create hybrid workflows. For example, normalize traces with a config, then use a user script to detect and annotate phase arrivals using custom logic.

# config.yaml
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'normalize'

Then:

surfquake process --config config.yaml --user_script annotate_picks.py

This feature makes SurfQuake highly adaptable for both research and operational seismic processing pipelines.

docs.title: Seismic Data Files
docs.text:
Seismic instruments record ground motion as a sequence of measurements through time. These measurements are stored in waveform files, which contain the digital samples of a seismic signal together with basic information needed to interpret their timing and acquisition. Depending on the sensor, the recordings may represent earthquakes, ambient seismic noise, controlled seismic sources, or other vibrations.

In SurfQuake / Integrated Seismic Program (ISP), waveform handling is based on ObsPy, a Python framework widely used in seismology. Consequently, SurfQuake can work with the seismic waveform formats supported by ObsPy, subject to the requirements of each particular SurfQuake workflow.

Waveforms and metadata are complementary

A waveform file contains the recorded samples and essential trace information, such as the channel identifier, start time, and sampling rate. Station metadata, often stored separately in StationXML, describe the station location, sensor orientation, and instrument response. Both are needed for many quantitative analyses. See the Metadata section for further information.

docs.title: Common seismic waveform formats
docs.text:
Several file formats are used in observational and exploration seismology. They differ in their structure, metadata fields, compression, and typical applications.

Format Common extension Description and typical use MiniSEED .mseed, .msd, .seed Compact, widely used waveform format for continuous monitoring and data exchange between seismic networks. A .seed extension alone does not establish the file type. SAC .sac Seismic Analysis Code format, commonly used for individual traces and earthquake or signal-processing studies. Includes an extensive waveform header. GSE2 .gse, .gse2 Exchange format for seismic waveform data, encountered in network archives and legacy datasets. SEGY .sgy, .segy Multi-trace format widely used for active-source seismic surveys and exploration. SEG2 .seg2, .dat Format often found in near-surface and engineering seismology, especially acquisition-system exports. Seismic Unix (SU) .su Trace-oriented format used in seismic exploration and processing workflows. Other supported formats Varies ObsPy also provides readers for formats such as SEISAN, AH, CSS, K-NET, and several instrument-specific formats.

MiniSEED is a good default for continuous seismic recordings, while SAC is particularly convenient when working with individual traces and their analysis headers. The appropriate choice depends on the dataset and processing objective.

File extensions do not guarantee the format

Filename extensions are conventions, not definitive identifiers. ObsPy usually detects the format from the file contents. Support for a format in ObsPy does not necessarily mean every SurfQuake feature accepts every possible file variant or acquisition-specific header.

For an authoritative list, consult the ObsPy waveform reading documentation.

docs.title: How waveform data are organized
docs.text:
ObsPy uses two principal objects to represent waveform recordings:

Object Description Main contents Stream Collection of one or more seismic traces. A set of Trace objects, possibly from different stations, components, or time intervals. Trace One regularly sampled time-series segment. Sample array (data) and a header (stats) with identifiers, timing, and sampling information.

A Stream may contain several traces, for example the vertical, north–south, and east–west components from one seismic station. The same channel may appear in multiple traces when a recording is divided into separate time segments.

ObsPy Stream
  ├── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHZ
  │     ├── data  → waveform samples
  │     └── stats → identifiers, timing, sampling rate
  ├── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHN
  │     ├── data
  │     └── stats
  └── Trace: XX.ABC.00.BHE
        ├── data
        └── stats
  • Identifying a seismic trace: NET.STA.LOC.CHA

Waveforms are commonly identified by four codes:

Network.Station.Location.Channel
   XX  .  ABC .   00   . BHZ
  • Network (XX): the seismic network.
  • Station (ABC): the recording station.
  • Location (00): identifies a particular sensor or data stream at the station; it may be empty.
  • Channel (BHZ): identifies the acquisition channel, including its component designation under the relevant naming convention.

These codes connect a waveform to the corresponding station and channel metadata. They do not, by themselves, specify the recording interval or guarantee that the instrument configuration remained unchanged.

docs.title: What information matters most?
docs.text:
• Sampling rate and recording time

Each regularly sampled trace has a sampling rate \(f_s\), measured in samples per second (Hz). The time interval between consecutive samples is

\[ \Delta t = \frac{1}{f_s}. \]

For example, at 100 Hz the interval between samples is 0.01 s. The theoretical Nyquist frequency is \(f_N=f_s/2\), although the frequency band that can be interpreted reliably also depends on the recording instrument and its acquisition filters.

A trace header normally includes its start time, sampling rate, and number of samples (npts). ObsPy uses these quantities to determine the time associated with each sample. Times are normally handled in UTC through UTCDateTime.

  • Data gaps, overlaps, and continuity

Continuous archives may contain gaps (missing time intervals), overlaps (repeated or conflicting samples), or segments with different sampling rates. These issues can affect filters, spectral analyses, event detection, and other processing methods.

Check continuity before signal processing

Do not assume that all files from one station form an uninterrupted record. Inspect missing intervals and overlaps before merging data. Filling gaps with zeros or interpolated samples changes the time series and can introduce artificial signal content.

  • Sample amplitudes and physical units

Seismic waveforms are often stored as digital counts. Counts are not necessarily displacement, velocity, or acceleration. Obtaining calibrated physical measurements generally requires the corresponding instrument response and an appropriate response-removal procedure.

For more details, see the Metadata section.

docs.title: Preparing waveform files for SurfQuake / ISP
docs.text:
Before importing data into a processing project, it is good practice to:

  • Confirm that the files can be read and contain the expected channels and time intervals.
  • Check the sampling rates and identify any gaps or overlaps.
  • Ensure that network, station, location, and channel identifiers are consistent.
  • Prepare matching StationXML or other compatible station metadata when station positions, orientation, or response corrections are required.
  • Preserve the original recordings and perform processing on separate copies when practical.

These checks are especially useful for continuous monitoring, earthquake waveform analysis, ocean-bottom seismometer recordings, and ambient-noise processing.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Seismic waveform files contain the recorded time series and their basic acquisition information. Different formats serve different applications, but SurfQuake / ISP benefits from ObsPy's common Stream and Trace interface for working with them.

MiniSEED and SAC are particularly common in observational seismology. Regardless of the format, reliable processing begins by checking trace identifiers, timing, sampling rates, continuity, and the availability of corresponding station metadata.

docs.title: Source Parameters

The tool Source Parameters is designed to estimate events source parameters (i.e., Mw, ML, seismic moment, corner frequency, radiated energy, source size and stress drop`) and the attenuation parameters (t-star, quality factor).

Info

It is based in the implementation of Satrinano et al., 2023. A detailed theoretical background can be found here

docs.title: Spectral Analysis Tools
docs.text: SurfQuake provides three main tools for spectral analysis of seismic data: spectrum, spectrogram, and CWT (Continuous Wavelet Transform). These tools enable users to inspect frequency content in different forms—static, time-evolving, and high-resolution wavelet representations.

docs.title: Spectrum
docs.text: The spectrum tool computes the frequency-domain representation of a single seismic trace using the multitaper method by default, which is robust against noise and spectral leakage.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• method: Spectral estimation method. Options:
  • multitaper (default)
  • fft or others if extended

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrum'
    method: 'multitaper' # 'fft' for conventional spectrum with single taper
    output_path: /Users/surf_test/spectral

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Amplitude vs. Frequency plot
  • Optional log-log or semi-log axes (loglog, xlog, ylog)
  • Serialized result saved as .sp

docs.title: Spectrogram
docs.text: The spectrogram method produces a time-frequency representation of a seismic trace using short-time Fourier Transform (STFT).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• win (float): Window length in seconds (e.g., 5.0)
  • overlap_percent (float): Percent overlap between windows (e.g., 50.0)
  • linf, lsup: Lower and upper frequency limits for plotting
  • method: Spectral estimation method. Options:
  • multitaper (default)
  • fft

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'spectrogram'
    method: 'multitaper'
    win: 5.0
    overlap_percent: 50.0
    output_path: /Users/surf_test/spectral

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Power over time and frequency in decibels (dB)
  • Plotted as a color-coded matrix
  • Serialized result saved as .spec

docs.title: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
docs.text: CWT provides high-resolution time-frequency analysis using scalable wavelets. Ideal for transient signals and high-precision timing.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• wavelet:
  • "cm": Complex Morlet (default and recommended for phase coherence)
  • "mh": Mexican Hat
  • "pa": Paul wavelet
  • param: Wavelet parameter (e.g., 6.0)
  • fmin, fmax: Frequency range (optional)
  • nf: Number of frequency bins

docs.title: Config Example
docs.text:
Analysis:
  process_1:
    name: 'cwt'
    wavelet: 'cm'
    param: 6.0
    fmin: 0.5
    fmax: 20.0
    nf: 80
    output_path: /Users/surf_test/spectral

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Scalogram in decibel power
  • Prediction masks showing reliable analysis range
  • Serialized result saved as .cwt

docs.title: Plotting and CLI Usage
docs.text:
All spectral results can be visualized via the CLI:

# Plot a spectrum
surfquake specplot --file path/to/file.sp

# Plot a spectrogram
surfquake specplot --file path/to/file.spec 

# Plot a wavelet scalogram with optional clipping
surfquake specplot --file path/to/file.cwt --type cwt --clip -120

# Save output to file
surfquake specplot -f file.spec --save_path output.png

docs.title: CLI Options
docs.text:
• --file, -f: Path to serialized .sp, .spec, or .cwt file
  • --type, -t: Type of spectral result to plot (spectrum, spectrogram, cwt)
  • --clip, -c: Optional clipping in dB for spectrogram or CWT
  • --save_path: Output path to save the figure

docs.title: Understanding and Accessing Spectral Result Objects in Python
docs.text:
SurfQuake does not store only an image of the spectral analysis. Its serialized output files contain Python result objects that preserve the numerical arrays and the original ObsPy Trace. This allows users to inspect spectral values, select particular frequencies or time windows, and perform further analysis without extracting data from a figure.

The examples below describe the classes implemented in specrun.py. The import path assumes that this module is installed as surfquakecore.data_processing.specrun; adjust it if your installation uses a different module layout.

docs.title: 1. Spectrum object (.sp)
docs.text:
A spectrum saved as .sp contains a TraceSpectrumResult instance. Its main attributes are:

Attribute Contents trace Original (or trimmed) ObsPy Trace, including waveform samples in trace.data. stats ObsPy trace metadata (starttime, sampling_rate, network, station, etc.). freq One-dimensional array of frequency samples in Hz. spectrum One-dimensional array of spectral amplitudes associated with freq. method Estimation method used, such as multitaper or fft. 
import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.data_processing.specrun import TraceSpectrumResult

result = TraceSpectrumResult.from_pickle("path/to/trace.sp")

print(result.trace.id)
print(result.stats.starttime)
print("Method:", result.method)
print("Frequency bins:", result.freq.shape)

frequency_hz = np.asarray(result.freq)
amplitude = np.asarray(result.spectrum)

# Read the amplitude at the frequency bin nearest to 5 Hz.
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(frequency_hz - 5.0))
print(f"{frequency_hz[idx]:.3f} Hz: {amplitude[idx]:.6g}")

The two arrays are paired by index: spectrum[i] corresponds to freq[i]. The stored values are spectral amplitudes, not a time-frequency matrix.

docs.title: 2. Spectrogram object (.spec)
docs.text:
A spectrogram saved as .spec contains a TraceSpectrogramResult instance. It preserves the original power matrix rather than only the decibel values displayed in the figure.

Attribute Contents trace Original ObsPy Trace. stats Trace metadata. time One-dimensional array of spectrogram time coordinates, in seconds relative to trace start. freq One-dimensional array of spectrogram frequencies, in Hz. spectrogram Two-dimensional power array, indexed as [frequency, time]. num_steps Number of computed time steps returned by the spectral calculation. 
import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.data_processing.specrun import TraceSpectrogramResult

result = TraceSpectrogramResult.from_pickle("path/to/trace.spec")

power = np.asarray(result.spectrogram)
frequencies = np.asarray(result.freq)
times = np.asarray(result.time)

print("Power matrix shape:", power.shape)
print("Frequency bins:", len(frequencies))
print("Time steps:", len(times))
assert power.shape == (len(frequencies), len(times))

# Power at the nearest available frequency and time bin.
fi = np.argmin(np.abs(frequencies - 2.0))
ti = np.argmin(np.abs(times - 60.0))
print(f"Power at {frequencies[fi]:.2f} Hz and {times[ti]:.1f} s:", power[fi, ti])

# Extract a frequency band (1–5 Hz) for subsequent calculations.
band = (frequencies >= 1.0) & (frequencies <= 5.0)
band_power = power[band, :]
print("Selected band matrix:", band_power.shape)

# Obtain absolute UTC times for the spectrogram columns.
absolute_times = [result.stats.starttime + float(t) for t in times]
print("First spectrogram time:", absolute_times[0])

Important distinction: result.spectrogram contains linear power values. The plotting method converts them to relative decibels, taking the maximum finite power as its reference:

\[ P_{\mathrm{rel}}(f,t) = 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{P(f,t)}{P_{\max}}\right). \]

You can reproduce the conversion in Python:

max_power = np.nanmax(power)
if not np.isfinite(max_power) or max_power <= 0:
    raise ValueError("Spectrogram has no positive finite maximum")

with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    relative_db = 10.0 * np.log10(power / max_power)

# Zero-power cells become -inf dB; filter them when needed.
finite_db = relative_db[np.isfinite(relative_db)]
print("Finite relative dB range:", finite_db.min(), finite_db.max())

The frequency and time coordinates describe the computed bins; they should not be confused with the waveform's individual sample times. Plotting options such as clip, split, and smooth change the presentation, not the stored power matrix.

docs.title: 3. Cross-spectral result object (.coh)
docs.text:
The same module also provides TraceCrossSpectralResult for analyses between a reference (input) trace and a target (output) trace. These objects can be saved as .coh files.

Attribute or property Contents ref_trace, trace Reference and target ObsPy traces. ref_stats, stats Metadata for the respective traces. freq Frequency samples in Hz. gxx, gyy Reference and target autospectral estimates. gxy Complex cross spectrum, defined as E[conj(X) * Y]. n_avg Averaging information used by the coherence-threshold calculation. method Spectral estimation method. coherence Derived magnitude-squared coherence (between 0 and 1). transfer Derived complex transfer function gxy / gxx. amplitude, phase_deg Derived transfer-function magnitude and phase in degrees. 
from surfquakecore.data_processing.specrun import TraceCrossSpectralResult

result = TraceCrossSpectralResult.from_pickle("path/to/pair.coh")

print("Input:", result.ref_trace.id)
print("Output:", result.trace.id)

frequency_hz = result.freq
coherence = result.coherence
transfer_function = result.transfer
magnitude = result.amplitude
phase_degrees = result.phase_deg

# Identify frequencies with coherence of at least 0.8.
reliable = coherence >= 0.8
print("High-coherence frequencies:", frequency_hz[reliable])

These last four quantities are computed from the stored spectral estimates when accessed; they are Python properties, not separate arrays serialized independently. High coherence measures a strong linear frequency-domain relationship, but does not by itself establish causality.

docs.title: 4. CWT result object (.cwt)
docs.text:
A Continuous Wavelet Transform is represented by TraceCWTResult, defined in surfquakecore.data_processing.cwtrun. Unlike the spectrogram object, the wavelet result keeps its transform and associated coordinates in a five-element tuple called cwt_data.

Attribute Contents trace Original ObsPy Trace, including waveform samples. stats Trace metadata (starttime, sampling_rate, channel, etc.). cwt_data[0] t: relative time coordinates in seconds. cwt_data[1] f: wavelet frequency coordinates in Hz, logarithmically spaced. cwt_data[2] scalogram: wavelet-transform values, indexed as [frequency, time]. cwt_data[3] pred: left-hand edge-effect boundary, expressed as relative time coordinates. cwt_data[4] pred_comp: right-hand edge-effect boundary, expressed as relative time coordinates.

Load a previously saved CWT result (the default serialization is gzip-compressed pickle):

import numpy as np
from surfquakecore.data_processing.cwtrun import TraceCWTResult

result = TraceCWTResult.from_pickle("path/to/waveform.cwt")

print("Trace:", result.trace.id)
print("Sampling rate:", result.stats.sampling_rate, "Hz")

times, frequencies, coefficients, left_edge, right_edge = result.cwt_data

print("Time coordinates:", times.shape)
print("Frequency coordinates:", frequencies.shape)
print("CWT matrix:", coefficients.shape)
assert coefficients.shape == (len(frequencies), len(times))

# Inspect a coefficient at the nearest sampled frequency and time.
fi = np.argmin(np.abs(frequencies - 2.0))
ti = np.argmin(np.abs(times - 60.0))
print("CWT coefficient:", coefficients[fi, ti])

Amplitude versus power: The stored scalogram is the output of ConvolveWaveletScipy.scalogram(). The CWT plotting method computes power as abs(scalogram)**2 and then displays power in decibels relative to the maximum:

power = np.abs(coefficients) ** 2
max_power = np.nanmax(power)
if not np.isfinite(max_power) or max_power <= 0:
    raise ValueError("CWT power must have a positive finite maximum")

with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    relative_db = 10.0 * np.log10(power / max_power)

# Extract CWT power between 1 and 5 Hz.
selected = (frequencies >= 1.0) & (frequencies <= 5.0)
band_power = power[selected, :]

The left_edge and right_edge arrays delimit regions near the beginning and end of the trace where wavelet edge effects can influence the interpretation. They are boundary coordinates, not Boolean masks. The implementation computes them using an auxiliary linearly spaced frequency vector, whereas the stored frequencies vector is logarithmically spaced; avoid treating the boundary arrays as exact per-bin validity flags without considering this distinction.

# Display the saved CWT using its built-in plotting method.
result.plot_cwt(split=1.0, clip=-80)

# Save a result object; the method chooses the .cwt filename.
result.to_pickle("./spectral_results", compress=True)

As with the other result objects, plotting parameters modify the figure presentation rather than replacing result.cwt_data. For the supported wavelet choices and computation parameters, see the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) section above.

docs.title: 5. Inspecting an object and saving results
docs.text:
All four classes implement to_pickle(folder_path, compress=True) and from_pickle(filepath, compress=True). Compression is enabled by default, so use the same compress setting when loading that was used when saving. File extensions (.sp, .spec, .coh, .cwt) identify the result type; they do not by themselves indicate whether gzip compression was enabled.

# Explore attributes of an object already loaded as `result`.
print(type(result))
print(vars(result).keys())

# Save the full object to a directory (file name assigned automatically).
result.to_pickle("./spectral_results", compress=True)

docs.title: Trace Header
docs.text:
SurfQuake processing and visualization tools make extensive use of the metadata embedded in ObsPy Trace objects (MiniSEED format). These headers not only contain acquisition-related data (station, channel, sampling rate) but are also extended during analysis to store arrival picks, reference markers, and more.

SurfQuake processing and visualization tools make extensive use of the metadata embedded in ObsPy Trace objects, which are often read from MiniSEED (MSEED) files. While MSEED is a widely accepted format for storing seismic time series, it is inherently read-only in terms of header modification—meaning users cannot persistently embed new metadata directly into the original file.

To overcome this limitation, SurfQuake dynamically extends the Trace.stats header in memory during processing and interaction. This enriched metadata includes not only core acquisition parameters like network, station, channel, and sampling rate, but also a wide array of analysis results such as:

Arrival picks from manual or automatic phase picking

Reference markers used for alignment or annotation

Geodetic attributes like source-receiver distance, backazimuth, and theoretical arrival times

Since these enhancements cannot be stored back into standard MSEED files, SurfQuake writes processed trace data to HDF5 (.h5) format. This format supports flexible, hierarchical storage and allows full preservation of the enriched metadata alongside waveform data—ensuring reproducibility, traceability, and compatibility with downstream processing.

By adopting HDF5 for intermediate and final outputs, SurfQuake enables a more transparent and integrated seismic analysis workflow, without losing critical contextual information during each stage of the pipeline.

This guide outlines the custom fields and their use cases for SurfQuake users.

docs.title: Core Header Fields (ObsPy Standard)
docs.text:
These fields are part of the default trace.stats dictionary and are typically populated during reading:

Field Description network Network code (e.g., IU, CI) station Station code (e.g., ANMO) location Location code (e.g., 00, 10) channel Channel name (e.g., BHZ, HHN) starttime Trace start time (UTCDateTime) endtime Trace end time (UTCDateTime) sampling_rate Sampling rate in Hz npts Number of points

docs.title: Header Info from Command Line
docs.text:
surfquake facilitates a tool to explore the information of your seismogram files. Supports standard and SurfQuake-extended headers such as picks, references, and geodetic attributes

surfquake -w [path to waveform files (e.g. './data/*Z or './mseed1,./mseed2] -c [Number of traces (columns) to show per file, default 1]

Example 

> surfquake info -w './ES.ELOB..HHZ.D.2018.233,./ES.EMAZ..HHZ.D.2018.233' -c 2

File                 | ES.ELOB..HHZ.D.2018.233   | ES.EMAZ..HHZ.D.2018.233  
Network              | ES                        | ES                       
Station              | ELOB                      | EMAZ                     
Location             |                           |                          
Channel              | HHZ                       | HHZ                      
Start Time           | 2018-08-21T00:12:58.4300  | 2018-08-21T00:12:56.3977 
End Time             | 2018-08-21T00:47:06.6900  | 2018-08-21T00:47:03.5077

docs.title: Trace header modification
docs.text:
If you need to modify the header of your traces, I recommend that you use quick or process_daily command and use the rename process. This process simply maps the original traces header information into the new one. Here, you will find an example of config file with the process of mapping network, station, location and channel codes.

Analysis:
  process_1:
      name: 'rename'

      networks:
        IM: IH      # Replace network XX → YY
        IK: IN

      stations:
        IL02: XX02
        ARNO: MELI

      channels:
        SHZ: BHZ     # Entire channel replacement

      components:
        Z: E         # Only the last component letter (Z → E, N → Z, etc.)

docs.title: SurfQuake-Extended Header Fields
docs.text: These fields are dynamically added during processing or interactive analysis:

docs.title: trace.stats.picks (list of dicts)
docs.text:
Stores manually or automatically picked phase arrivals.

Each entry contains: - time (float): UTC timestamp of the pick - phase (str): Picked phase (e.g., P, S, Lg) - amplitude (float): Measured amplitude at pick time - polarity (str): U (up), D (down), or ?

{
  "time": 1727123830.321,
  "phase": "P",
  "amplitude": 3.21e-05,
  "polarity": "U"
}

docs.title: trace.stats.references (list of float)
docs.text: Stores timestamps marking user-defined reference lines during plotting (e.g., using keypress w). These are used for alignment, cross-checking picks, or beamforming time tags.

docs.title: trace.stats.geodetic
docs.text:
Stored during preprocessing via set_header_func:

Field Description distance Source-receiver distance (km) baz Backazimuth from station to source (°) az Azimuth from source to station (°) incidence Theoretical incidence angle (°) arrivals Dict of theoretical arrival times per phase name (UTC timestamp)

docs.title: Example:
docs.text:
trace.stats.geodetic = {
    "distance": 254.7,
    "baz": 123.4,
    "az": 303.4,
    "incidence": 31.5,
    "arrivals": {
        "P": 1727123829.20,
        "S": 1727123844.03
    }
}

docs.title: During Processing
docs.text:
• Headers are updated by processing steps such as:
  • shift: aligns data using theoretical or picked times
  • rotate: may use geodetic data to perform LQT rotations
  • beamforming: may store attributes related to time or azimuth reference

docs.title: During Plotting
docs.text:
• Interactive actions modify headers:
  • Press e: Add pick to trace.stats.picks
  • Press w: Add reference marker to trace.stats.references
  • Press d or p: Remove the last pick or reference
  • Press m: Remove all reference lines

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Pick and reference data are stored in-memory and optionally exported to CSV.
  • Ensure that when traces are saved or passed between steps, trace.stats is retained.
  • You can inspect or modify these attributes using standard Python syntax: 
    trace.stats.picks.append({...})
trace.stats.references = []

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• You can add custom metadata to trace.stats for later use (e.g., annotations, flags, temporary calculations).
  • You can modify waveform data directly, apply filters, or normalize traces.
  • You can access event and station metadata for context-aware processing.
  • Changes made in the user script are preserved if the output is saved to HDF5 or passed through the pipeline.

This flexibility makes SurfQuake an ideal platform for advanced, reproducible seismic workflows tailored to your research or operational needs.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: These headers extend the utility of MiniSEED traces in SurfQuake workflows by embedding processing history and interactive annotations, making the data more portable and self-descriptive across analysis steps.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text: In this section we show some useful utilities to make easier how to create a metadata file and manage a catalog.

docs.title: Create Metadata from CLI
docs.text:
The csv2xml tool allows users to generate StationXML metadata required by SurfQuake modules.

It supports two common scenarios:

  1. Only station coordinate file available → A valid StationXML is generated with default channel information.
  2. Station file + RESP/Inventory files available → Full response information is incorporated automatically.

docs.title: Minimum Required Station File
docs.text:
The station table must contain at least the following columns:

Net Station Lat Lon elevation start_date starttime end_date endtime

Example (space-separated or CSV format supported):

WM ARNO 37.0988 -6.7322 117.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM AVE 33.2981 -7.4133 230.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
WM CART 37.5868 -1.0012 65.0 2007-01-01 00:00:00 2050-12-31 23:59:59
  • Columns are case-insensitive.
  • The tool automatically detects whitespace or comma-separated files.
  • Date format must follow:

<!-- -->
YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS

Start/end times can be wide ranges (e.g., 2007 → 2050).

If no channel information is provided, a default channel is created: - Channel code: HHZ - Sample rate: 100.0 Hz

docs.title: Optional Columns (Advanced Metadata)
docs.text: The tool automatically uses additional columns if present.

docs.title: Station-Level Optional Columns
docs.text:
Column Name Description

site_name Human-readable station name

clock_drift Clock drift rate (seconds/second). Applied to all channels unless overridden

docs.title: Channel-Level Optional Columns
docs.text:
Column Name Description

channel Channel code (e.g., HHZ, HHN, HHE)

location_code SEED location code

sample_rate Sampling rate (Hz)

dip Channel dip (degrees)

azimuth Channel azimuth (degrees)

depth Sensor depth (meters)

clock_drift Channel-specific drift (overrides station-level drift)

If multiple rows exist for the same station with different channels, all channels will be included in the StationXML.

docs.title: Using RESP / Inventory Files
docs.text:
If a RESP (or StationXML inventory) directory is provided:

  • The tool scans recursively.
  • All channels found in RESP files are indexed by: (Network, Station, Location, Channel)
  • If the CSV does not specify channels, RESP channels are used automatically.
  • If the CSV specifies channels, matching RESP responses are attached when available.

RESP files must correspond to the correct Network and Station codes.

docs.title: Command Line Usage
docs.text: surfquake csv2xml     -c [csv_file_path]     -r [resp_files_path]     -o [output_path]     -n [stations_xml_name]

docs.title: Required Arguments
docs.text:
• -c, --csv_file_path → Path to station table
  • -o, --output_path → Directory for output StationXML
  • -n, --stations_xml_name → Output filename

docs.title: Optional Argument
docs.text: • -r, --resp_files_path → Directory containing RESP/Inventory files

docs.title: Interactive Help
docs.text: surfquake csv2xml -h

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The updated csv2xml tool now:

  • Accepts whitespace or comma-separated files
  • Validates numeric and date fields
  • Supports multi-channel stations
  • Integrates RESP metadata robustly
  • Supports OBS clock drift metadata
  • Applies intelligent defaults when optional columns are missing

This makes metadata creation flexible, robust, and suitable for both simple deployments and advanced OBS workflows.

docs.title: Run Create Metadatafrom CLI
docs.text: >> surfquake csv2xml -c ./stations_file.txt -r ./resp_files_folder -o ./output_path -n metadata.xml

docs.title: Build MTI config files
docs.text: surfQuake core library incorporates and easy way to generate mti Config Files The only thing you need is a previously crated catalog and a mti.ini files that serves of template (just copy and paste the example in the explanation of config file from MTI). The routine will create the mti.ini files using the information from the event catalogs (date, latitude, lngitude, depth and magnitude) and from the rest of the fields from the template. This action will write a mti.ini file per event and ready to be used by MTI toolbox.
